a: the journey up from Babylon began
p: The Hebrew vowels make the date the start of the journey. The Greek reads the same letters as "he fixed" it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (vowels יְסֻד, yesud); KJV
readings.en: that was the beginning of the going up from Babylon
readings.plain: the journey up from Babylon began

readings.w: Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked: αὐτὸς ἐθεμελίωσεν τὴν ἀνάβασιν; the same Hebrew letters read יִסַּד (yissad)
readings.orig: αὐτὸς ἐθεμελίωσεν τὴν ἀνάβασιν τὴν ἀπὸ Βαβυλῶνος
readings.en: he himself founded (fixed) the going up from Babylon
readings.plain: he set the start of the journey up from Babylon

why: The Masoretic vowels give good sense, and the dates are the same either way. The Greek, which needs only different vowels, makes Ezra the one who fixed the day; many commentators prefer it, and the note on 7:8 gives the dates.

a: Of the descendants of Zattu, Shecaniah son of Jahaziel
p: The Hebrew lacks the clan name. Both Greek versions have Zattu, a clan of the first return.

readings.w: Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ζαθοης Σεχενιας υἱὸς Αζιηλ); 1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 8:32 (ἐκ τῶν υἱῶν Ζαθοης Σεχενιας Ιεζηλου); the BHS apparatus proposes it; most modern translations
readings.orig: ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ζαθοης Σεχενιας υἱὸς Αζιηλ
readings.en: of the sons of Zathoes, Sechenias son of Aziel
readings.plain: Of the descendants of Zattu, Shecaniah son of Jahaziel

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: of the sons of Shecaniah, son of Jahaziel
readings.plain: Of the descendants of Shecaniah son of Jahaziel

why: Every other entry names a clan and then its leader. Both Greek translations, made from Hebrew copies far older than the Leningrad Codex, have Zattu here, the clan of 2:8 and 10:27. One of them is the literal 2 Esdras, which usually agrees with the Masoretic Text even where the Hebrew is hard, so its agreement with the freer 1 Esdras here carries weight. The word most likely dropped out of the Hebrew by accident. The Plain English Translation follows the Greek here and keeps the Hebrew form of the other names.

a: Of the descendants of Bani, Shelomith son of Josiphiah
p: As at 8:5, the Hebrew lacks the clan name; both Greek versions have Bani.

readings.w: Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (καὶ ἀπὸ υἱῶν Βαανι Σαλιμουθ υἱὸς Ιωσεφια); 1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 8:36 (ἐκ τῶν υἱῶν Βανι Ασσαλιμωθ Ιωσαφιου); the BHS apparatus proposes it; most modern translations
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπὸ υἱῶν Βαανι Σαλιμουθ υἱὸς Ιωσεφια
readings.en: and of the sons of Baani, Salimouth son of Josephia
readings.plain: Of the descendants of Bani, Shelomith son of Josiphiah

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: and of the sons of Shelomith, son of Josiphiah
readings.plain: Of the descendants of Shelomith son of Josiphiah

why: The same reasoning as at 8:5: the list's pattern needs a clan, Bani is a clan of the first return (2:10), and both Greek translations have it. The Hebrew probably lost the word because "Bani" (בני) looks like the word before it, "sons of" (בני).

p: The margin of the Hebrew reads Zaccur; the written text has Zabbud.

readings.w: Qere (the reading in the margin of the Masoretic Text)
Ketiv (the written text of the Masoretic Text); KJV

why: The two names look alike in Hebrew letters. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere in each Ketiv-Qere pair in these chapters (8:14, 8:17 twice, 10:2, 10:29, 10:35, 10:37, 10:43, 10:44), since it is the reading the Masoretes passed on for public reading.

t: "I commanded" or "I sent out" (Ketiv and Qere)
p: The margin reads "I commanded them"; the written text has "I sent them out."

readings.w: Qere (margin of the Masoretic Text)
Ketiv (written text of the Masoretic Text); the KJV combines both ("I sent them with commandment")

why: Both make sense, and the meaning hardly changes. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, as elsewhere. The same verse has a second pair ("those given" / "the temple servants"); see the note on Iddo's kinsmen.

p: The Masoretic vowels read "his brother" (singular). The same letters can be read "his brothers," as the Greek versions have it.

readings.w: The Hebrew letters revocalized אֶחָיו (echav), "his brothers"; Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (πρὸς τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς αὐτῶν, "to their brothers"); 1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 8:46 (8:45 in Rahlfs: Αδδαιω καὶ τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς αὐτοῦ, "to Addaios and his brothers"); KJV ("to his brethren"), BSB and most modern translations
readings.en: to Iddo, his brothers the temple servants

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (vowels אָחִיו, achiv)
readings.en: to Iddo his brother, the temple servants

why: Here the Plain English Translation leaves the Masoretic Text, as it does at 8:5, 8:10 and 10:3, and the case is argued, not assumed. As vocalized, the Hebrew puts a singular "his brother" in apposition to a plural, "the temple servants," which does not construe; the only way to keep it is to supply an unnamed second man. Changing only the vowels gives "his brothers," which fits the plural that follows and the message sent to a group. Both Greek translations, one of them the literal 2 Esdras, read a plural, and so did the KJV's translators. The Plain English Translation adds "and" for English, since Iddo heads the group he is sent to.

p: The Hebrew has 77 lambs. 1 Esdras has 72 in Codex Alexandrinus, a multiple of twelve like the other numbers, and 76 in Codex Vaticanus.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern translations

1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 8:63 (8:66 in KJV numbering), with Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes) and the KJV ("threescore and twelve lambs"); Codex Vaticanus (Swete) has 76 (ἄρνας ἑβδομήκοντα ἕξ), which the site's 1 Esdras follows

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew. 72 (six times twelve) fits the pattern of the other offerings so neatly that it could be the original or a later tidying; there is no way to be sure.

p: The Hebrew and 2 Esdras end the list with the Amorites; 1 Esdras has the Edomites.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (ὁ Αμορι)
1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 8:66 (8:69 in KJV numbering): Ιδουμαίων; Hebrew behind it הָאֲדֹמִי (reconstructed)

why: Without vowels, "Amorite" (אמרי) and "Edomite" (אדמי) share three letters, alef, m and y; Amorite has r after the m, where Edomite has d before it. So r and d, which look almost alike in Hebrew script, stand in different places, and a change from one word to the other needs more than one misread letter. The Amorites belong to the list of Canaan's nations in Deuteronomy 7:1, which the officials are drawing on. "Edomites" would match Deuteronomy 23:7, where Edomites and Egyptians are named together. 1 Esdras also lacks the Ammonites. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and the more literal Greek.

p: The same Hebrew letters can mean "my lord" (Ezra) or "the Lord" (God). The Masoretic vowels say God.

readings.w: Hebrew letters read אֲדֹנִי (adoni), "my lord"; supported by Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (ὡς ἂν βούλῃ, "as you wish") and 1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 8:90 (8:94 in KJV numbering: ὡς ἐκρίθη σοι, "as was decided by you"); KJV and most modern translations; the 2 Esdras reading also turns the next clause into a command (see below)
readings.en: by the counsel of my lord

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (vowels אֲדֹנָי, Adonai); NJPS keeps it ("the Lord")
readings.en: by the counsel of the Lord

why: Shecaniah is speaking to Ezra, and both Greek translations understood "you." The Masoretic vowels may express reverence, or a reading of the plan as God's own counsel. The consonants are the same, so the choice is between two old interpretations, and the versions are not unanimous: NJPS keeps the Masoretic "the Lord."
b: 2 Esdras 10:3–4 also reads the next words differently. Where the Hebrew has "and of those who tremble (vehacharedim) at the command of our God," the Greek has an imperative addressed to Ezra, "Arise, and make them tremble at the commands of our God," which fits its "as you wish" before it. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew in that clause.

t: "He went there" or "He spent the night there"?
p: The Hebrew and 2 Esdras say Ezra went there; 1 Esdras says he spent the night there.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (וַיֵּלֶךְ); Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (καὶ ἐπορεύθη ἐκεῖ); KJV
1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 9:2 (καὶ αὐλισθεὶς ἐκεῖ); Hebrew behind it וַיָּלֶן (reconstructed); several modern translations

why: "He went there" repeats the verse's earlier "went," which looks clumsy, and "spent the night" differs in Hebrew by one letter, so many scholars prefer 1 Esdras. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew, which the literal Greek of 2 Esdras also had.

p: The Hebrew says four men "stood against" (or "over") the plan. The two Greek versions both make them helpers.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (עָמְדוּ עַל־זֹאת); most modern translations
Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (μετ᾽ ἐμοῦ περὶ τούτου); Hebrew behind it perhaps עִמִּי, "with me" (reconstructed)
1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 9:14 (ἐπεδέξαντο κατὰ ταῦτα), a free rendering of the Hebrew; compare the KJV "were employed about this matter"

why: The Hebrew most naturally means opposition, and an objection is the harder reading, the kind a later copyist would smooth away. The Greek versions both turn the men into supporters, perhaps for that reason. See the note on this phrase.

a: Ezra the priest and certain men, heads of families from each ancestral house, all of them named, were set apart
p: The Hebrew has "Ezra... and men were set apart"; 1 Esdras has "Ezra chose for himself men."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (וַיִּבָּדְלוּ); Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (καὶ διεστάλησαν Εσδρας ὁ ἱερεύς); KJV
readings.orig: וַיִּבָּדְלוּ עֶזְרָא הַכֹּהֵן אֲנָשִׁים רָאשֵׁי הָאָבוֹת
readings.en: and Ezra the priest, men, heads of the fathers, were set apart
readings.plain: Ezra the priest and certain men, heads of families from each ancestral house, all of them named, were set apart

readings.w: 1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 9:16 (καὶ ἐπελέξατο ἑαυτῷ Εσδρας ὁ ἱερεὺς ἄνδρας); Hebrew behind it וַיַּבְדֵּל לוֹ (reconstructed); RSV, NRSV
readings.orig: καὶ ἐπελέξατο ἑαυτῷ Εσδρας ὁ ἱερεὺς ἄνδρας ἡγουμένους
readings.en: and Ezra the priest chose for himself leading men
readings.plain: Ezra the priest chose for himself certain men, heads of families from each ancestral house, all of them named

why: The Hebrew is awkward, but 2 Esdras read the same text. 1 Esdras gives smoother sense with a small change of the verb ("he separated for himself"). The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew; either way Ezra and the family heads form the court.

p: The Hebrew names Malchijah twice in one clan. Both Greek versions have Hashabiah the second time.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV

Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (Ασαβια); 1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 9:26 (Ασιβιας); Hebrew behind it חֲשַׁבְיָה (reconstructed; the BHS apparatus proposes it)

why: Two men of the same name in one clan is possible, so the Hebrew may be right. But both Greek translations agree on Hashabiah, and a copyist could easily repeat a name from earlier in the line. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew with this doubt noted.

p: The margin reads "and Ramoth"; the written text has Jeremoth.

readings.w: Qere (margin of the Masoretic Text); KJV; compare Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (Ρημωθ)
Ketiv (written text of the Masoretic Text); BSB

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, as in the other Ketiv-Qere pairs. The written text's Jeremoth is a common name in this list (10:26, 10:27).

p: The written text and the margin differ, and the Leningrad Codex mixes them.

readings.w: Qere (margin of the Masoretic Text): כְּלוּהוּ; KJV (Chelluh)
Ketiv (written text of the Masoretic Text): כלהי
The Leningrad Codex's mixed form, the vowels of the Qere on the letters of the Ketiv; ESV, BSB

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, as in every other Ketiv-Qere pair in these chapters. Many English versions print "Cheluhi," which reads the Qere's vowels on the written letters, a form no scribe intended to be read aloud.

p: The margin reads Jaasai, the written text Jaasu. The Greek of 2 Esdras read the letters as a verb, "and they did."

readings.w: Qere (margin of the Masoretic Text)
Ketiv (written text of the Masoretic Text); KJV (Jaasau), BSB (Jaasu)
Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (Μαθαναι, καὶ ἐποίησαν), reading the written letters as the verb וַיַּעֲשׂוּ

why: The written letters can be a name or the verb "they did." In a list of names a name is far more likely. The Plain English Translation follows the Qere.

t: Two names, or a new clan?
p: The Hebrew reads "Bani, Binnui." The Greek of 2 Esdras reads "the sons of Binnui," starting a new clan.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV

Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked (οἱ υἱοὶ Βανουι καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ Σεμεϊ); Hebrew behind it וּמִבְּנֵי בִנּוּי (reconstructed; the BHS apparatus proposes it); BSB, NRSV
readings.orig: οἱ υἱοὶ Βανουι καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ Σεμεϊ
readings.en: the sons of Binnui and the sons of Shimei
readings.plain: Of the descendants of Binnui: Shimei,

why: The Greek makes good sense: Bani's list (10:34–37) would end, and a new clan, Binnui's (compare Nehemiah 7:15), would begin. The Hebrew letters for "and Bani" and "and of the sons of" are close. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew, but the Greek may well be right; it would make the total 111 men rather than 113.

p: The margin reads Jaddai; the written text has Jaddo.

readings.w: Qere (margin of the Masoretic Text); BSB
Ketiv (written text of the Masoretic Text); KJV (Jadau)

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Qere, as in the other Ketiv-Qere pairs in these chapters.

a: Some of them had wives by whom they had had children.
p: The Hebrew is hard. 1 Esdras says the men sent the wives away with their children; 2 Esdras says they had fathered sons.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (וְיֵשׁ מֵהֶם נָשִׁים וַיָּשִׂימוּ בָּנִים); KJV
readings.en: and there were among them women, and they placed (had) sons
readings.plain: Some of them had wives by whom they had had children.

readings.w: 1 Esdras (Esdras A, the freer Greek parallel), Rahlfs' text, checked, 9:36 (the same number in the KJV): καὶ ἀπέλυσαν αὐτὰς σὺν τέκνοις; RSV, NRSV; the BHS apparatus and Rudolph reconstruct a Hebrew text behind it
readings.en: and they sent them away with children
readings.plain: They sent them away, with their children.

readings.w: Septuagint, 2 Esdras (Esdras B, the literal Greek of Ezra–Nehemiah), Rahlfs' text, checked: καὶ ἐγέννησαν ἐξ αὐτῶν υἱούς
readings.en: and they fathered sons from them
readings.plain: And they had fathered sons by them.

why: The Hebrew is difficult but can be read. 2 Esdras, the literal Greek, had much the same text and smoothed it. 1 Esdras, a freer version, gives an ending that reports the dismissal; it may preserve a different Hebrew, or it may be completing the story. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: The verse also has a Ketiv-Qere pair: the written text has nos'e, "takers of," the margin nas'u, "they had taken." The Plain English Translation follows the margin. On the meaning of the whole verse, see the note.
